Brief History of Halloween

Most of us view Halloween, or “Trick-or-Treat, as a sweet holiday. After all, what other holiday are you going to get a bagful of free candy?

But Halloween’s history began a Celtic festival of Samhain (pronounced sow-in) that’s rooted in a fear of malicious spirits. More than two centuries ago, the Celts believed the boundary between the living and the dead blurred at the start of the cold, dark winter on October 31st. On that date, The Celts lit bonfires, sacrificed animals and wore animal heads and skins ward off or hide from those roaming ghosts.

In the 8th century, Pope Gregory III moved All Saints Day, which honored saints and martyrs to November first, and the Celtic rituals were folded in with bonfires and dressing up as saints, angels and devils on All Hallows’ Eve, which transformed into the word, Halloween. But underpinning the modern religious and secular versions of this holiday is the spiritual world that many still believe exists..

According to a YouGov poll, nearly half of U.S. adults – 46% – believe in ghosts.

So, the means asking a question that seems surreal: are ghosts real?
